title: World-Telling
text:
Little child, suddenly here,

you who did not come, yet arrived,

I shall tell you what we possess,

and you will take your share from ours.
editorial_note: The coined title preserves Mistral's fusion of counting and telling the world into being.

title: Dusk
text:
I feel my heart, in sweetness,

melting away like wax:

my veins are a slow oil,

and not wine,

and I feel my life slipping away,

silent and gentle as the gazelle.
editorial_note: Kept the sacramental contrast between oil and wine and the poem's quiet deceleration.

title: Finding
text:
I came upon this child

as I walked toward the fields:

I found him there asleep

among the heads of wheat…


Or perhaps it happened

as I crossed the vineyard:

reaching for a vine leaf,

I brushed against his cheek…


And that is why I fear,

when I fall asleep,

he may vanish like

the frost upon the vines…
editorial_note: The translation keeps the maternal wonder and the final image's fragile, evaporating cold.

title: The Stars Are Children in a Ring…
text:
The stars are children in a ring,

playing at spying on the earth…

The wheat stalks are the waists of girls,

playing at swaying…, swaying…


The rivers are children in a ring,

playing at meeting in the sea…

The waves are girls dancing in a ring,

playing at embracing Earth…
editorial_note: Ronda is rendered as a children's ring game, preserving both circular motion and play.

title: The Sea Rocks Its Thousands of Waves…
text:
The sea rocks its thousands of waves,

divine.

Hearing the loving seas,

I rock my child.

The wandering wind in the night

rocks the wheat.

Hearing the loving winds,

I rock my child.

God the Father rocks his thousands of worlds

without a sound.

Feeling his hand in the darkness,

I rock my child.
editorial_note: Repeated rock preserves the lullaby's physical rhythm and its widening movement from cradle to cosmos.

title: The Peacock
text:
The wind blew and carried off the clouds,

and in the clouds a peacock sailed,

and the peacock was meant for my hand,

and my hand is going to wither away,

and this morning I gave that hand

to the king who came to make me his bride.


Oh, the sky, oh, the wind, and the cloud

that drift away with the peacock!
editorial_note: The cumulative and keeps the ballad-like spell while sailed makes the peacock's impossible passage vivid.

title: Night Is Desolation…
text:
Night is desolation

from the mountains to the sea.

But I, the one who rocks you,

I am not alone!


The sky is desolation

if the moon falls into the sea.

But I, the one who holds you close,

I am not alone!


The world is desolation

and the flesh goes sorrowing.

But I, the one who clasps you,

I am not alone!
editorial_note: Desamparo is kept as desolation rather than mere loneliness, preserving its sense of abandonment and exposure.

title: Tenderness
text:
Mother mine,

tender little mother,

let me tell you

the sweetest words.


This body is yours,

you gathered it like a bouquet;

let me tumble it

across your lap.


You pretend to be a leaf

and I will be the dew;

and in your wild arms

hold me hanging there.


Mother mine,

my whole entire world,

let me tell you

my deepest endearments.
editorial_note: Diminutives are carried through intimate syntax rather than repeated literal littleness; the floral and play imagery remains tactile.

title: Now That I Am a Queen, Though Once a Beggar…
text:
Now that I am a queen, though once a beggar,

I live in naked fear that you will leave me,

and pale, I ask you, every passing hour:

“Are you still with me? Oh, do not go far!”

I would like to make the journey smiling,

trusting now that you have come;

but even in my sleep I lie afraid

and ask you in my dreams: “Have you not gone?”
editorial_note: The royal and destitute selves remain in tension; marchas becomes the shared journey rather than a literal march.

title: Sleep, Sleep, My Own Dear One…
text:
Sleep, sleep, my own dear one,

free of trouble, free of fear,

though my soul itself may not sleep,

though I may find no rest.


Sleep, sleep, and through the night

may you make less sound

than the blade of grass,

than the fleece's silk.


May my flesh sleep within you,

my trouble and my trembling.

Let my eyes close within you:

may my heart sleep within you!
editorial_note: Dueño mío is rendered as intimate possession without the harshness of owner; the repeated sleep retains the lullaby cadence.
